33 -- # Basics: Functional Programming in Lean

5--- The *functional style* of programming is founded on simple mathematical
6--- intuitions: A program is essentially a concrete means for computing a
7--- mathematical function, which just maps inputs to outputs. Even when
8--- programs have side effects, such as reading or writing files or network
9--- packets, these side effects can be given a mathematical characterization
10--- (such as through the use of monads). This connection between programs and
11--- mathematical functions makes it possible to reason both precisely and
12--- formally about a program's behavior, i.e., to *prove properties* about
13--- programs.
14-
15--- This functional style is one sense of the word "functional" in "functional
16--- programming." The other sense is that it emphasizes the use of functions as
17--- *first-class* values — i.e., values that can be passed as arguments to
18--- other functions, returned as results, included in data structures, etc. The
19--- recognition that functions can be treated as data gives rise to a host of
20--- useful and powerful programming idioms.

24+-- The *functional style* of programming is founded on simple, everyday
25+-- mathematical intuitions: If a program has no side effects, such as reading
26+-- or writing files or network packets, then (ignoring efficiency) all we need
27+-- to understand about it is how it maps inputs to outputs. That is, we can
28+-- think of it as just a concrete means for computing a mathematical function.
29+-- This direct connection between programs and simple mathematical objects
30+-- supports both formal correctness proofs and sound informal reasoning about
31+-- program behavior. This is one sense of the word "functional" in "functional
32+-- programming."
33+
34+-- The other sense in which functional programming is "functional" is that it
35+-- emphasizes the use of functions as *first-class* values -- i.e., values
36+-- that can be passed as arguments to other functions, returned as results,
37+-- included in data structures, etc. The recognition that functions can be
38+-- treated as data gives rise to a host of useful and powerful programming
39+-- idioms.

425--- such symbols. Simply type `\` (backslash) followed by the name of the

427--- with the actual symbol. For example, typing `\all` or `\forall` will
428--- produce `∀` and `\->` or `\to` will produce `→`. To find out what backslash
429--- sequence produces a unicode symbol that you can see on the screen, just
430--- hover over it. To see all of the Unicode shortcodes, open the Command
431--- Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS), type "Lean
432--- 4: Show Unicode Input Abbreviations", and press Enter.

11161089 -- ### The `rewrite` tactic
11171090 
1118--- The `rewrite` tactic tells Lean to rewrite (part of) a goal or hypothesis
1119--- based on a rule (or rules), given in square brackets. For example, given
1120--- the rule `add_zero`, which states that `n + zero` is equal to `n` for any
1121--- `n`, we can replace any `n + zero` in our proof with `n` via
1122--- `rewrite [add_zero]`.
1091+-- As we saw above, the tactic that tells Lean to rewrite (part of) a goal or
1092+-- hypothesis based on a rule is called `rewrite`. Given the rule `add_zero`,
1093+-- which states that `n + zero` is equal to `n` for any `n`, we can replace
1094+-- any `n + zero` in our proof with `n` via `rewrite [add_zero]`.
1095+
1096+-- The `rewrite` tactic takes its argument(s) in square brackets.
11231097 
11241098 -- ### The `rfl` tactic
11251099 
11261100 -- The `rfl` tactic closes a goal of the shape `a = a`, for any `a`. It checks
1127--- that both sides of the equality are *definitionally equal* — that is, that
1101+-- that both sides of the equality are *definitionally equal* -- that is, that
11281102 -- they reduce to the same term. (So, in particular, a term is always
11291103 -- definitionally equal to itself.)
11301104

11511125   rfl

11571131 -- ### Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof Engineering
11581132 
11591133 -- Lean, like any other programming language, has conventions and best
1160--- practices for writing good software. Lean takes inspiration from
1161--- object-oriented programming in favoring the use of *encapsulation*. In OOP,
1162--- it is considered poor style to expose the fields of an object in its
1163--- interface; instead, those fields should only be accessible by an object's
1164--- methods (like getters and setters). Doing so hides the object's definition,
1165--- so that, if its fields or implementation ever change, the interface it
1166--- exposes to the outside world remains the same.
1167-
1168--- In idiomatic Lean, it is similarly considered poor style to "peek" through
1169--- definitions by using `rfl` to implicitly simplify expressions that aren't
1170--- syntactically identical. If you take a look at the proofs of `add_zero` and
1171--- `add_succ` above, you will notice this is exactly what we did when we used
1172--- the `rfl` tactic.
1134+-- practices for writing good software. In object-oriented programming, for
1135+-- example, it is considered good practice not to access the fields of an
1136+-- object directly, but instead to use getter and setter methods. This helps
1137+-- to encapsulate the object's definition, so that, if its fields or
1138+-- implementation ever change, the interface it exposes to the outside world
1139+-- remains the same. In simple examples such conventions may seem trivial or
1140+-- even silly; in complex codebases, it is the only way to maintain crucial
1141+-- invariants that prevent a system from becoming unmaintainable.
1142+
1143+-- The same principle applies to definitions and proofs in Lean. In idiomatic
1144+-- Lean, it is considered poor style to "peek" through definitions by using
1145+-- `rfl` to implicitly simplify expressions that aren't syntactically
1146+-- identical. If you take a look at the proofs of `add_zero` and `add_succ`
1147+-- above, you will notice this is exactly what we did when we used the `rfl`
1148+-- tactic.
11731149

16951712 -- ### More on Notation (Optional)
16961713 
16971714 -- Lean has a very flexible notation system. Operators like `+` and `*` are
16981715 -- defined with specified precedence and associativity. For example, `+` has
16991716 -- precedence 65 and is left-associative, while `*` has precedence 70 and is
1700--- also left-associative. This means that `1 + 2 * 3 * 4` is parsed as
1701--- `1 + ((2 * 3) * 4)`.
1717+-- also left-associative. This means that `1+2*3*4` is parsed as
1718+-- `1+((2*3)*4)`.
17021719 
17031720 -- You can define custom notation using the `notation`, `infixl`, `infixr`,
17041721 -- `prefix`, and `postfix` commands.
17061723 -- Lean handles notation scoping through namespaces and *type classes*. The
17071724 -- numeric literal `3` can be interpreted as `Nat`, `Int`, `Float`, etc.,
17081725 -- depending on the expected type, thanks to Lean's `OfNat` type class. We
1709--- will explain type classes in more detail in the Typeclasses chapter.
1726+-- will explain type classes in more detail in the `Typeclasses` chapter,
1727+-- found in `Typeclasses.lean`.

17211743 -- When Lean checks this definition, it verifies that the recursion
17221744 -- terminates. Specifically, it checks that one of the parameters is

5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6--- variable with no constraint on it:
5+-- So far we have discussed **parametric polymorphism**, where in Lean we can
6+-- declare a type variable
77 
88 variable (α : Type)

10--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks  @mwhicks1):
11---     Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
12---     lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
13---
14---     `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`

21--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
22--- `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
23--- which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
24--- `a : α`.
25-
26--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α` completely
27--- generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean, this is done
28--- through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept
29--- originated in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from other
30--- languages, such as traits in Rust.
31-
32--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
33-
34--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
35--- occurs in a list:
36-
10+-- without any further information about the details of the type `α`. Here we
11+-- are able to work with a type like `List α`, and can write functions like
12+-- `List.reverse` or `List.length` that only operate on the structure of a
13+-- list independently of its contents. Along with these we have corresponding
14+-- proofs like `List.length_reverse` that are similarly structural in nature.
15+
16+-- This is somewhat limiting, as we cannot inspect or non-trivially use any
17+-- particular `a : α`. What we might want in some situations rather than `α`
18+-- being completely generic is to partially specify its behavior. In Lean,
19+-- this happens through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called
20+-- **typeclasses**. This concept originated in the Haskell programming
21+-- language, and is analogous to features you may be familiar with in other
22+-- languages such as traits in Rust.
23+
24+-- ## First Example: Inhabited Types
25+
26+-- Suppose we wanted to specify that a type has at least one inhabitant —
27+-- i.e., that it is not empty. We have previously seen `structure`, which
28+-- would allow us to express this as
29+
30+structure HasOneStruct (α : Type) where
31+  one : α
32+
33+-- As discussed previously, a structure is just an inductive type that comes
34+-- with a single constructor, in this case `HasOneStruct.mk`, along with a few
35+-- different syntaxes for convenience:
36+
37+def nat_hasOneStruct_mk : HasOneStruct Nat := HasOneStruct.mk 1
38+
39+def nat_hasOneStruct_brace : HasOneStruct Nat := {one := 1}
40+
41+def nat_hasOneStruct_where : HasOneStruct Nat where
42+  one := 1
43+
44+-- All of these are the same value, a structure of type `HasOneStruct Nat`
45+-- that we can thing of as carrying a piece of data (a term that is not a
46+-- proposition), the number `1`, as evidence that this type is not empty. We
47+-- can use this in proofs such as
48+
49+theorem nat_hasOneStruct_eq_one : nat_hasOneStruct_mk.one = 1 := rfl
50+
51+-- to see how this structure provably contains the value that we have placed
52+-- within it. In Lean, typeclasses work very similarly, and in fact are
53+-- implemented as structures. The only difference in defining a typeclass is
54+-- that we instead use the `class` keyword:
55+
56+class HasOne (α : Type) where
57+  one : α
58+
59+-- While the definition is essentially the same, including the constructor
60+-- `HasOne.mk`, the usage of typeclasses is different, and what allows us to
61+-- use them to express ad hoc polymorphism. Instead of using `def` to define
62+-- inhabitants of this type, we will instead use the `instance` keyword:
63+
64+-- Note to developers:
65+--     From GitHub (@chenson2018): Part of the point here is that we don't
66+--     usually refer to instances explicitly, even me providing an explicit
67+--     name is for pedagogy reasons. I'll make it more explicit in the text
68+--     that what we're looking for in the infoview is the presence of this
69+--     instance.
70+
71+instance instHasOneNat : HasOne Nat where
72+  one := 1
73+
74+-- The definition is exactly the same as above (and any of the alternative
75+-- syntaxes work as well), but instead of being used as a definition that we
76+-- pass around, Lean will try to infer its usage through a process called
77+-- **typeclass synthesis** or **typeclass inference**. To help see this, let's
78+-- define another instance of `HasOne` for `Int`, the type of integers ... -2,
79+-- -1, 0, 1, 2, ...
80+
81+instance instHasOneInt : HasOne Int where
82+  one := -1
83+
84+-- Instead of explicitly referring to a structure like we did in the proof
85+-- `nat_hasOneStruct_eq_one`, we can instead use `HasOne.one`, and Lean will
86+-- use typeclass inference to determine the intended meaning. As an example,
87+-- you can write
88+
89+example : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
90+example : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
91+
92+-- and based on the type annotations Lean will infer which of these instances
93+-- you intended to use. So these proofs are equivalent to
94+
95+example : instHasOneNat.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
96+example : instHasOneInt.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
97+
98+-- but without needing to explicitly refer to the instances `instHasOneNat`
99+-- and `instHasOneInt`. Another way that we can inspect what instance is being
100+-- using with the constructor of a typeclass is the option `pp.all`. For
101+-- example looking at
102+
103+set_option pp.all true in
104+example : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
105+
106+set_option pp.all true in
107+example : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
108+
109+-- we can see that `@HasOne.one Nat instHasOneNat` and
110+-- `@HasOne.one Int instHasOneInt` are the respective terms that appear on the
111+-- right hand side of each equality.
112+
113+-- Lean also has a command `#synth` that allows you to search for an instance
114+-- of a given type. So the command
115+
116+#synth HasOne Nat
117+
118+-- for instance prints `instHasOneNat`, informing us that this is the instance
119+-- found that has type `HasOne Nat`. In general, the assumption is that for
120+-- typeclasses like `HasOne` that include data, as opposed to solely proofs,
121+-- that these these instances should be unique to avoid ambiguity.
122+
123+-- Note to developers:
124+--     @chenson2018: I don't really want to explain diamonds here, is the

127+-- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
128+
129+-- Notably, the above examples enforce no conditions on the data that they
130+-- carry, and we could provide any value that we would like for `HasOne.one`.
131+-- This could be misleading, for instance if we had instead defined an
132+-- instance
133+
134+sf_experiment
135+  instance : HasOne Nat where
136+    one := 2
137+
138+-- we might have some counterintuitive proofs based on the name leading us to
139+-- believe the class contained the element `1`. In most languages that support
140+-- typeclasses it is not possible to enforce a notion of "lawfulness" as part
141+-- of the typeclass, and it falls to the author to ensure that any desired
142+-- invariants are satisfied.
143+
144+-- As an example, suppose that we wanted to express the idea that a type has
145+-- at least two distinct elements. A first attempt might be
146+
147+sf_experiment
148+  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
149+    one : α
150+    two : α
151+
152+-- but this does not disallow the case where `one` and `two` are equal. In a
153+-- proof assistant, however, typeclasses can also carry proofs along with
154+-- data, so we can write
155+
156+class HasTwo (α : Type) where
157+  one : α
158+  two : α
159+  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
160+
161+-- to enforce that these are two distinct entries. Declaring instances works
162+-- in much the same way as before, except that now `HasTwo.one_neq_two`
163+-- requires a proof:
164+
165+instance : HasTwo Nat where
166+  one := 1
167+  two := 2
168+  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
169+

188+class HasThree (α : Type) where

190+  two : α
191+  three : α

75--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the function
76--- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify

79--- Rust. Particular implementations of that class, different ones for
80--- different types, are called *instances*. For functions that would use such
81--- instances, we specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit* on the
82--- polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies to. This directs
83--- Lean to rely on the class inside the function, and to find and fill in the
84--- appropriate instance when the function is called.

442--- are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
443--- of this representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view of maps,
444--- as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to
445--- every query in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
446--- function, rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies
447--- proofs that use maps.
